story1046:
In the time before time had a name, when the world was still learning its own shape, there lived a man called Kanati — The Lucky Hunter — and his wife Selu, whose name meant Corn. They were the first Cherokee man and woman, and they lived together in a house at the edge of a great forest where the mountains rose like the backs of sleeping bears.

Kanati was a hunter beyond all other hunters. Each morning he would rise before the sun and walk to the mouth of a cave that lay beneath a great stone outcropping. There, where the rock met the earth like a half-closed eye, he would place his hand upon a flat stone that sealed the entrance. When he moved that stone, an animal would emerge — deer, bear, or rabbit — and Kanati would strike it down with his spear. The people marveled at his skill, for he never missed and never returned empty-handed.

But there was a mystery to Kanati's hunting that no one understood. The animals that emerged from the cave were strange in their behavior — they walked as if dazed, their eyes glassy and unfocused, as if they were dreaming while awake. The elders whispered about this, but none dared speak openly, for Kanati was generous with his kills and shared the meat with everyone in the village.

Selu, too, had a secret. When the people were hungry, she would stand before them and rub her stomach, and kernels of corn would fall from her body like rain. She would rub her sides, and beans would tumble to the ground in cascading streams. The people feasted, and they called her generous, but they did not know where the food truly came from.

Now Kanati and Selu had a son, and the boy grew strong and curious. One day, while hunting in the deep woods, he found a strange child — a Wild Boy, feral and naked, with matted hair and sharp teeth. The Wild Boy had been born, the people said, from the blood of the animals that Kanati killed, for when the blood of the slain beasts pooled upon the earth, it sometimes rose up in the shape of a child.

The two boys became inseparable. They hunted together, played together, and shared the secrets of the forest. But the Wild Boy was clever in ways that were not entirely good, and he began to wonder about Kanati's cave. Why did the animals emerge so docilely? What lay behind the great stone?

One evening, when Kanati was away and Selu slept, the boys crept through the forest to the cave. The Wild Boy urged the son forward, and together they pushed aside the great stone. Inside, they found not a den of beasts but a vast underground world — and there, chained to the walls, were all the animals of the earth, every species, every kind, waiting to be released one by one.

The boys' eyes went wide. But in their wonder, they made a terrible mistake. The Wild Boy reached out and broke the chains. One by one, the animals fled into the forest — deer, bear, wolf, rabbit, all of them running free. The boys tried to catch them, but the animals were too many and too fast. By morning, every creature had escaped.

When Kanati discovered what had happened, his face was grave. "Now the animals will hide from us," he said. "They will run when they hear our footsteps. We will have to chase them through the forest and the mountains, and sometimes we will go hungry. This is the way of things now." And so it was that the Cherokee learned to hunt — not with ease, but with effort, tracking their quarry through the wild places of the earth.

But the story of Selu was sadder still. The boys, frightened by their father's anger, told their mother what they had done. Selu listened quietly, and when they finished, she said, "I know what will happen to me now." For she knew that her secret — the corn that came from her body — would be discovered.

She told the boys to drag her body seven times around a cleared circle of earth, and then seven times inside the circle. "When you have done this," she said, "corn will grow by morning, and the people will never hunger."

The boys did as she asked, but in their grief and haste, they did not complete the ritual properly. They dragged her body six times around the circle and six times within it. When morning came, corn did grow — but only in certain places, only in certain soils. It did not cover the earth as Selu had intended.

And so the Cherokee learned both the gift and the limitation of corn. They learned that generosity has a price, that secrets once broken cannot be unbroken, and that even the most sacred gifts may be diminished by human error. But they also learned that Selu's love endured in every stalk that rose from the earth, every kernel that filled their baskets in the autumn. Corn was her body, and beans were her bounty, and in the harvest, the Cherokee honored her memory.
story1047:
In the time before the earth had settled into its final form, when all was water and darkness and the sky hung low like a stone vault above the primordial sea, there lived the animals in a world of mist and shadow. They had no ground beneath their feet, no mountains to climb, no forests to shelter in — only the stone ceiling of the sky world above and the black water below.

Among these creatures was a tiny being called Dâyuni'sï — the Water Beetle — no larger than a child's thumbnail, with a shell like polished obsidian and legs that moved with tireless patience. While the larger animals — Bear, Deer, Wolf, and the great birds — hovered at the edges of the sky world, peering down at the water with unease, it was the Water Beetle who volunteered.

"I will go down," said Dâyuni'sï, and the others looked at him with doubt. How could such a small creature accomplish what the mighty could not? But the Water Beetle did not wait for their approval. He dove beneath the surface of the water and disappeared.

He dove deep — deeper than any creature had ever gone — through darkness so complete that even his own eyes were useless. He swam with the certainty of one who knows that the answer lies not in sight but in touch. At the very bottom of the ocean, his legs found something soft — mud, wet and yielding, clinging to him like a living thing.

Dâyuni'sï gathered the mud in his claws and began the long journey back to the surface. It was a difficult ascent, for the mud was heavy and the water pushed against him, but the Water Beetle was patient and persistent. When he finally broke through the surface, he carried the mud to the animals and placed it before them.

"Plant this on the back of the Great Turtle," they said, for in those days a great turtle floated on the surface of the sea, his shell broad as an island.

The animals placed the mud upon the turtle's back, and it began to grow. It spread outward in every direction, swelling and rising like bread dough, covering the turtle's shell until the land extended far beyond what any eye could see. The earth was soft and flat, unmarked by mountains or valleys, and the animals rejoiced.

But the earth was not yet complete. The Great Buzzard — a bird so large that his wingspan blocked the sun — flew down from the sky world to survey the new land. He was the mightiest of the flying creatures, with feathers like hammered copper and eyes that could see a mouse from the height of the clouds.

The Great Buzzard flew low over the earth, his great wings beating the air. As he flew over what would become the Cherokee homeland — the mountains of North Carolina, Tennessee, and Georgia — his wingtips struck the soft ground. Where his left wing touched the earth, it rose up in a ridge of mountains. Where his right wing dipped, a valley was carved. Again and again his wings swept the land, and the mountains rose and the valleys deepened.

The other animals watched from the sky with growing alarm. The land was becoming too rough, too broken by peaks and gorges. "Call him back!" they cried. "Before he makes the whole earth into mountains!"

And so the Great Buzzard was called back, his work unfinished but his mark forever upon the land. The Cherokee mountains stand steep and proud because of his wings, and the valleys between them run deep and shadowed. The ridges that run like the backbone of the earth are the imprints of his feathers.

When the land was settled and the mountains stood in their places, the Holy People set the sun upon a track — a path of light that would cross the sky each day from east to west, warming the earth and causing the corn to grow. They set the moon in her own orbit, pale and silver, and scattered the stars across the darkness of night like embers from a sacred fire.

The animals descended from the sky world and took their places upon the earth. Bear claimed the deep forests. Deer chose the mountain meadows. Wolf took the ridges and the riverbanks. Each creature found its home in the world that the Water Beetle had begun and the Great Buzzard had shaped.

And at the center of it all, in the heart of the Cherokee mountains, the land was good — rich with game, blessed with streams, sheltered by ancient forests. The Cherokee say that this is no accident. The Holy People made the world with care, and the Southern Appalachian homeland was made with the most care of all.
story1048:
In the deep rivers and dark lakes of the Cherokee homeland, beneath the surface where the light grows thin and the water turns cold as a dead man's hand, there lives a creature so terrible that even the bravest warriors speak its name in whispers. This is Uktena — the Horned Serpent — a being of immense power and ancient malice, coiled in the depths like a living thunderstorm.

Uktena is vast beyond imagining. Its body is thicker than the trunk of the oldest oak, covered in scales that shimmer with an unnatural light — each scale a different color, like the facets of a gemstone catching fire. From its head rise two great horns, curved and sharp as scythes, and between those horns, set into the center of its forehead, burns the Ulûñsû'tî — a crystal of blazing light, diamond-bright and pulsing with power. Those who look upon it say it resembles a large scarlet bead, and it is said that whoever possesses the Ulûñsû'tî gains the power of second sight — the ability to see what is hidden, to know what is true.

But Uktena's gaze is death. To look into its eyes is to feel the soul freeze within the body, to be rooted to the spot like a sapling struck by lightning. Those who meet its stare are paralyzed with terror, unable to flee, unable to fight, as the great serpent glides closer through the water, its massive body displacing the current like a living dam.

The first Uktena was not always a serpent. The elders tell that in ancient times, there was a man — a warrior of great pride and terrible ambition — who believed he could kill the sun. He climbed to the highest peak, the tallest mountain that pierced the sky, and hurled his spear at the blazing disk. The spear fell back, of course, as all things fall back when thrown against the eternal. But the sun, angered by this presumption, struck the man down and transformed him — his limbs stretching into coils, his skin hardening into scales, his eyes blazing with the fire he had sought to destroy. And so the first Uktena was born, a creature of rage and power, doomed to dwell in the dark waters forever.

Generations of Uktenas followed, each one spawned from the corruption of the first. They spread through the waterways of Cherokee territory — into the deep pools of the rivers, into the lakes that lay like dark mirrors in the mountain hollows, into the underground streams that carved their way through the limestone bones of the earth.

Only the bravest hunters and medicine men dared to seek out an Uktena, and they did so not for glory but for the crystal. The Ulûñsû'tî held power beyond measure — it could grant visions, reveal hidden truths, and protect its bearer from harm. But the crystal was also dangerous, for its power was not meant for mortal hands, and those who possessed it sometimes found that the visions it granted were more curse than blessing.

The most famous hunt for Uktena is told in hushed tones around the winter fires. A young medicine man — his name has been lost to time, as is the way with such stories — set out to find an Uktena that had been terrorizing the people of a remote mountain village. For three days he tracked the creature, following the signs that only a medicine man could read: the water that ran warm when it should have been cold, the fish that floated belly-up on the surface, the strange phosphorescent glow that rose from the river at midnight.

On the fourth night, he found the Uktena coiled beneath a great rock in the riverbed. Its scales cast an eerie light across the water, and the crystal in its forehead blazed like a captive star. The medicine man felt the pull of the creature's gaze — felt his muscles tighten, his thoughts slow, his will begin to dissolve. He closed his eyes and sang the songs of protection that his teacher had taught him, songs older than the mountains themselves.

Blind but singing, he plunged his spear into the soft place beneath the serpent's jaw. The Uktena thrashed, its massive body churning the river into a maelstrom, but the medicine man held fast. When the creature finally lay still, he cut the crystal from its forehead and carried it home.

The crystal brought him power — the ability to see illness before it manifested, to know the hearts of those who approached him, to speak with the spirits of the dead. But the crystal also brought loneliness, for the visions never stopped, and the medicine man found that knowing too much was its own kind of suffering. In time, he hid the Ulûñsû'tî in a place that no one has found, and it is said that the crystal still waits there, in the dark, burning with its quiet fire.

The Cherokee say that Uktena still dwells in the deep waters, and that on certain nights, when the moon is new and the river runs black, you can see its glow reflected on the surface — a point of scarlet light, pulsing like a heartbeat, deep beneath the waves.
story1049:
There are the people you see, and then there are the people you do not see. The Cherokee have always known this. Beside us, around us, sometimes passing through us like wind through a reed flute, are the Nunnehi — 'The Travelers' — also called 'Those Who Live Anywhere.' They are a race of spirit people, invisible to ordinary eyes, who dwell in the mountains and forests of the Cherokee homeland. They are not ghosts. They are not dreams. They are a people, complete and ancient, who share the earth with us but inhabit it differently.

The Nunnehi are beautiful in their spirit form — tall and regal, with the bearing of great warriors and the calm eyes of those who have seen the world change and change again. When they choose to reveal themselves to humans, they appear as Cherokee men and women dressed in the finest clothing, their faces serene, their movements fluid and deliberate. They are said to be larger than ordinary people, broader in the shoulder and longer in the limb, as if they were made from a more generous measure of the same clay.

Travelers in the deep mountains sometimes hear the Nunnehi before they see them — or rather, before they almost see them. The sound of singing drifts through the forest, voices harmonizing in melodies that no mortal choir could produce. Drums beat in rhythms that match the pulse of the earth itself. The music comes from inside hollow mountains, from caves that seem to have no end, from places where the rock opens like a doorway and then closes again.

One story tells of a war party — Cherokee warriors returning from battle in the north, weary and battered, their numbers too few to face the enemy again. They made camp in a narrow valley, and as they sat around their fire, they heard singing. The sound was beautiful and strange, rising from the earth itself. Several warriors followed the sound to the mouth of a cave, and there they were greeted by Nunnehi warriors — great men, taller and stronger than any they had ever seen, who invited them inside.

The Cherokee warriors entered the cave and found a world within — a great hall lit by firelight, with people dancing and feasting. The Nunhehi treated them as honored guests, gave them food and medicine, and told them to rest. When the warriors emerged the next morning, the cave was gone and the valley was empty. But when they returned to their people, they found that years had passed in the world outside. Children had become elders. Elders had died. The village had moved to a new location, and the warriors were the only ones who remembered the old ways.

The Nunnehi are generous with those who respect them. They have been known to return lost hunters to safety, to guide travelers through mountain passes in storms, to leave gifts of food at the doors of families in need. They borrow tools from villagers — pots, knives, baskets — and always return them clean and polished, often with small gifts of thanks tucked inside.

But the Nunhehi are not to be trifled with. Those who mock them, who speak their secrets aloud, who enter their dwellings without invitation, find themselves lost in the forest, walking in circles until they collapse from exhaustion. The Nunhehi do not punish cruelty with cruelty — they simply withdraw, and in their withdrawal, the world becomes a lonelier, colder place.

There is a story of a woman who wandered too close to a Nunhehi dwelling in the mountains. She heard the singing and followed it, step by step, deeper into the forest. The Nunhehi saw her and, recognizing her gentle spirit, invited her inside. She spent what felt like a single night in their company, listening to their stories, eating their food, watching their dances. But when she returned home, she found that her children had grown and gone, her husband had remarried, and the world she knew had moved on without her.

She told her story to the elders, and they shook their heads. "You should not have stayed so long," they said. "Time moves differently in the land of the Nunhehi." But the woman did not regret her visit, for she had seen things that no other mortal had seen — the true shape of the mountains, the faces of the spirits who dwell within them, the songs that the earth sings when no one is listening.

The Nunnehi are everywhere and nowhere. They walk the ridges at dawn. They dance in the caves at midnight. They are the travelers who never stop, the people who live anywhere because the whole world is their home. And if you are quiet enough, and still enough, and if your heart is open to the possibility, you may hear their singing — faint and beautiful, rising from the hollow mountains of the Cherokee world.
story1050:
In the deepest parts of the forest, where the canopy is so thick that the sun reaches the ground only in thin, golden threads, and the moss grows soft as a child's blanket over the rocks and roots — there live the Yunwi Tsunsdi, the Little People of the Cherokee. They are small, no taller than a young child, with quick eyes and quicker feet, and they have dwelt in the woods since the world was new.

The Yunwi Tsunsdi are invisible to most people. They move through the forest like shadows through water, appearing and disappearing at will. But they sometimes reveal themselves to those they trust — to children who wander too far from the village, to hunters who show respect for the forest, to medicine men who know the songs that open the doors between worlds.

They live in caves beneath mossy rocks, in hollow trees, in the spaces between roots where the earth is dark and warm. Their dwellings are not like ours — they are pocket-sized, scaled to their bodies, furnished with acorn cups and pine needle mats. The Yunwi Tsunsdi are great dancers and musicians, and on certain nights — nights when the moon is bright and the wind is still — you can hear their music rising from the ground: tiny drums, tiny flutes, voices pitched higher than a cricket's song.

The Little People are helpful to those who respect them. They have been known to lead lost hunters back to the trail by placing bright leaves along the path, or by singing in a direction that draws the wanderer toward home. They have blessed certain shamans with knowledge of healing herbs, appearing to them in dreams and showing them the plants that cure fever, ease pain, and close wounds.

Sometimes the Yunwi Tsunsdi borrow things from the village. They take a pot here, a knife there, always returning them clean and sometimes leaving a gift — a perfectly carved stone, a bundle of sweet grass, a handful of berries so ripe they glow like jewels. The people have learned not to be alarmed by these borrowings, for the Little People always give back more than they take.

But the Yunwi Tsunsdi are easily angered by disrespect. Those who mock them, who boast of having seen them, who chase them through the forest in pursuit of a story to tell — these people find themselves in trouble. The Little People do not harm mortals directly, but they have ways of making life difficult. They lead hunters astray. They scatter the crops in the field. They whisper bad dreams into the ears of those who sleep.

There is a story of a young man who boasted that he had seen the Yunwi Tsunsdi and described them to everyone who would listen. The Little People heard his boasting and were offended. That night, the young man went to fetch water from the spring and could not find his way home, though the spring was only a hundred paces from his door. He walked in circles for hours, hearing laughter in the trees, until dawn broke and the spell was lifted. He never boasted again.

Medicine men who work with the Yunwi Tsunsdi speak of them with reverence and caution. They say that the Little People possess knowledge that was lost when the world changed — knowledge of plants that no longer grow, of songs that no human voice can reproduce, of the true names of things. To earn their trust, a medicine man must spend years in the forest, learning its rhythms, respecting its creatures, showing through action rather than words that he is worthy.

Those who encounter the Yunwi Tsunsdi rarely discuss the experience directly. They speak in vague terms — "I was in the forest" or "I heard something" — but they do not describe what they saw. This silence is not fear but respect. The Little People share their world with those who are ready, and the best way to show you are ready is to listen more than you speak.

In the Cherokee way, the Yunwi Tsunsdi remind us that we are not alone in the forest, that the world is more populated than our eyes can see, and that the smallest beings may possess the greatest power. They are the keepers of the old knowledge, the guardians of the wild places, and the friends of those who walk softly upon the earth.
story1051:
She is called Nûñ'yunu'ï — Spearfinger — and she walks the ridges of the Great Smoky Mountains with a step that shakes the stones. She is a witch, a monster, a thing of ancient terror, and she has haunted the eastern mountains since before the Cherokee learned to plant corn.

Spearfinger's body is a horror. She stands taller than any human, gaunt andangular, her skin the gray-brown of old granite. She wears a dress of stone — not a dress made to look like stone, but a dress that is stone, heavy and cold, clicking against itself as she moves. The stone dress makes her nearly invulnerable; arrows glance off it, spears shatter against it, and even fire seems reluctant to touch her. Her face is the worst of her — gaunt, with hollow cheeks and a mouth that is always stained red with the blood of her victims.

But her most terrible feature is her right forefinger. It is long and sharp, extending from her hand like a spear point carved from obsidian. With this finger, Spearfinger cuts open her victims and eats their livers. She prefers the livers of children — their sweetness, their tenderness — and she will go to any length to get them.

The horror of Spearfinger is not only her physical power but her cunning. She can mimic the voices of loved ones — mothers, fathers, grandparents, dear friends. She stands at the edge of a village in the twilight, hidden among the trees, and calls out in a voice that sounds exactly like a child's mother: "Come home, little one. Come home." And the child, hearing that familiar voice, walks toward it. The other villagers hear nothing. By the time they realize what has happened, the child is gone.

Families lived in terror of Spearfinger. Mothers tied red threads around their children's wrists as protection. Fathers kept fires burning all night. But Spearfinger was patient, and she was clever, and eventually she found her way to every village in the mountains.

The elders called a council. The greatest warriors and medicine men gathered to discuss what could be done. A young warrior — brave, clever, and desperate — volunteered to track the creature to its lair. He followed the trail of missing children, the signs that only a medicine man could read: the stone dress that left marks on the ground, the blood that stained the rocks where she rested.

The trail led to a high ridge, a place of wind and stone, where the mountains dropped away on both sides into valleys filled with mist. There, in a cave beneath an overhang of dark rock, the warrior found Spearfinger sleeping, her stone dress clicking softly in her dreams, her terrible finger folded against her chest.

He raised his bow. But a medicine man had told him the truth: arrows could not pierce the stone dress. The only vulnerable spot on Spearfinger's body was a small point on the palm of her right hand — the place where the stone dress did not cover, where the flesh was soft and unprotected.

The warrior drew his bow and aimed. His first arrow struck the stone dress and shattered. His second struck the stone and flew to pieces. Spearfinger woke with a scream that echoed off the mountains, and she lunged at him with her spear-finger, the stone dress rattling as she moved.

He dodged, rolled, and came up with a second bow. He aimed not at her body but at her hand — at the small, soft point on her palm where the stone dress ended. The arrow flew true. It struck her palm, and Spearfinger shrieked — a sound like rock splitting — and fell from the ridge, tumbling down the mountainside, her stone dress breaking apart as she fell.

The warrior climbed down to where she lay. The stone dress was shattered, and beneath it, Spearfinger was nothing — a gray dust that the wind scattered across the mountain. The children she had taken were gone, their spirits released. And from that day, the ridges of the Great Smoky Mountains were safe again.

But the elders warned: Spearfinger's dress was made of stone, and stone endures. In certain places, on certain nights, when the wind blows cold and the moon is dark, you can hear the clicking of stone on stone — soft, rhythmic, patient — as if something is gathering itself back together in the dark.
story1052:
There are those who prey on the living, and then there are those who prey on the dying. The Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï — the Raven Mockers — are the most feared beings in the Cherokee world, for they come when you are weakest, when the breath is leaving your body, and they steal what little life you have left.

During the day, a Raven Mocker looks like anyone else. It might be the quiet man who lives at the edge of the village, or the woman who sells herbs at the market, or the elder who nods at you from the doorway. There is nothing in their faces that betrays them — no fang, no claw, no visible mark. But look closely, and you will see something wrong. Their eyes are sleepless, red-rimmed, with a depth of exhaustion that never fades no matter how much they rest. They look like people who have been awake for years, because in a sense they have. Every night, when the village sleeps, the Raven Mockers fly.

At night, the Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï transform. Their human skin falls away like a snake shedding its coat, and beneath it is something terrible — a body that is neither bird nor human, with long, ragged wings that beat the air with a sound like rushing wind, and talons that glow faintly in the darkness. They fly to the homes of the dying, drawn by the scent of departing life like vultures to carrion.

When a Raven Mocker reaches the home of its victim, it circles the house, its wings casting shadows that flicker like flames. Inside, the sick person feels a crushing weight on their chest, a cold that no fire can warm. The Raven Mocker reaches through the walls — through wood, through stone, through the fabric of the living world — and takes the remaining years of the dying person's life. It steals them like a thief stealing corn, drawing them out in pale, luminous threads that the creature absorbs into its own body.

The Raven Mockers eat the hearts of the dead. After the last breath has been drawn and the spirit has departed, the creatures tear open the chest and consume the heart, which they believe holds the essence of a person's remaining years. By eating the heart, the Raven Mocker adds those years to its own寿命, living far beyond the span of any mortal.

The only defense against a Raven Mocker is a medicine man who knows the proper rituals — songs of protection, herbs that create a barrier of sacred smoke, prayers that call upon the Thunder Beings for strength. Some medicine men could see the Raven Mockers even in their human form, recognizing them by their sleepless eyes and the faint smell of death that clung to their clothing. These medicine men would warn families when a Raven Mocker was near, and they would stand vigil at the bedsides of the dying, singing the songs that kept the creatures at bay.

But not all medicine men could see them, and not all families could afford the protection. The Raven Mockers were most active in times of plague and hardship, when death was common and the medicine men were spread thin. In those dark times, the creatures flew in packs — three, five, seven at a time — their wings beating the night sky into a frenzy, their cries mixing with the wind until the whole mountain seemed to howl.

The Cherokee speak of the Raven Mockers with a reverence that borders on terror. They are not simply monsters — they are a reminder that death is not always a clean break, that there are forces that feed on suffering, that the boundary between life and death is not a wall but a doorway, and that doorway has guardians who are not kind.

To this day, when someone in a Cherokee community falls gravely ill, the elders gather. They do not speak of Raven Mockers directly — that would give them power — but they light the sacred fire, burn the cleansing herbs, and sing the old songs. They stand watch through the long nights, and they do not leave until the sick person either recovers or has passed beyond the reach of the Kâ'lanû Ahkyeli'skï.

The Raven Mockers still fly. They fly on the darkest nights, when the moon is new and the clouds are thick, and their wings make no sound that human ears can hear. But the medicine men hear them. They always hear them.
story1053:
When the sky darkens and the thunder rolls across the mountains like the drums of war, the Cherokee do not cower. They listen. They stand at their doorways and look to the west, where the storm comes from, and they say, "The Aniyvdaqualosgi are riding."

The Thunder Beings — Aniyvdaqualosgi, or Ani-Yuntikwalaski — are among the most powerful spirits in the Cherokee world. They are not abstractions, not metaphors, not the random collisions of atmospheric forces. They are beings — alive, conscious, and purposeful — who ride the storm clouds in forms so magnificent that the human eye can barely hold them.

The greatest of the Thunder Beings is the Great Thunder, known as Galun'lati. He is human in form, unlike the bird-shaped thunder spirits of many other tribes. He stands at the center of the storm, dressed in lightning and rainbows, his body crackling with energy, his eyes flashing with the fire that men call lightning. Beside him ride his two sons — the Thunder Boys — younger and fiercer, their voices splitting the sky like axes splitting wood.

The Thunder Beings live in the west, above the sky vault, in a land where the clouds are solid ground and the rain falls upward. Their house is built of living lightning, its walls pulsing with color, its roof a dome of perpetual thunder. There, in the land above the world, they prepare for their journeys across the earth.

When the Thunder Beings ride, the sky transforms. Clouds gather like armies, dark and massive, their bellies purple with stored lightning. The wind rises, carrying the smell of rain and the electric charge that makes the hair stand on end. Then the first thunder cracks — not a rumble but a report, sharp and absolute, as if the sky itself had been split open with a blade.

Lightning is the fire from the Great Thunder's eyes. It strikes the earth with purpose — not randomly, not randomly, but with the precision of a hunter's arrow. It strikes the places that need cleansing, the trees that harbor evil spirits, the rocks where malevolent forces have gathered. When the lightning strikes, it leaves behind the smell of ozone and the faint outline of the Thunder Being's handprint, burned into the stone.

The priests of the Cherokee pray to the Thunder Beings for rain and blessings. They build altars on the high ridges, where the storms pass closest to the earth, and they lay offerings of tobacco and white bead. They sing the songs that the Thunder Beings taught the first medicine men — songs of power, songs of petition, songs that ride the wind like birds.

But not all Thunder Beings are friendly. The lesser Thunderers — those who live closer to the earth, in the cliffs and waterfalls and mountain clefts — are more dangerous. They are mischievous, sometimes cruel. They hurl rocks from the cliffs. They stir up flash floods. They send lightning to strike the unwary. The priests warn that these lesser spirits must be propitiated with offerings and respect, for they are jealous and easily angered.

There is a story of a man who climbed to the top of a waterfall during a storm, seeking to steal a feather from the Great Thunder's headdress. The Thunder Boys saw him and were amused at first, for no mortal had ever been so bold. But when the man reached for the feather, the Great Thunder turned his gaze upon him, and the man felt the full weight of the storm — the wind, the rain, the lightning, the thunder — pressing down on him like the palm of a giant hand.

The man fell from the waterfall and was killed. His body was found at the base of the falls, unmarked by lightning but twisted in a way that suggested he had been squeezed by something impossibly large. The priests said that the Great Thunder had granted him a swift death, which was more mercy than he deserved.

The Thunder Beings are neither good nor evil. They are power — raw, elemental, and ancient. They bring the rain that makes the corn grow and the lightning that purifies the air. They are the warriors of the sky, the defenders of the cosmic order, and the friends of those who approach them with humility and respect. When the storm comes, the Cherokee stand at their doorways and watch, and they remember that the world is bigger than they are, and more powerful, and that the beings who ride the clouds are watching over them.
story1054:
In the beginning, the only fire in the world belonged to the Thunders, who lived in the sky world above. Fire was their treasure, their sacred gift, and they kept it burning on the great hearth of the heavens, where it crackled and popped and sent sparks spiraling upward into the darkness. The Thunders guarded their fire jealously, for without it, the sky world would be as cold and dark as the earth below.

The animals of the earth shivered in the cold. They had no fire to warm themselves, no fire to cook their food, no fire to light the darkness. The nights were long and bitter, and the animals gathered in caves and hollows, huddled together for warmth, their breath rising in pale clouds.

At last, the animals called a council. They met in a clearing beneath the bare winter trees, and they debated who should go to the sky world to steal fire from the Thunders. Many volunteered. Many failed.

Raven went first. He was proud and strong, with wings that could carry him above the clouds. He flew to the sky world and found the Thunders' fire burning on the great hearth. He seized a burning ember in his talons and flew back toward the earth, but the ember was hot — hotter than anything Raven had ever touched. His feathers turned black, charred by the heat, and he dropped the ember into the sea. Raven flew home with his feathers ruined and his pride in tatters.

Screech Owl went next. He was small and quick, and he thought he could snatch a coal without being burned. He flew to the sky world and crept close to the fire. He reached out with his foot and touched the ember — and the heat seared his eyes, turning them the deep red they remain to this day. He dropped the coal and flew home blind in one eye.

Hooting Owl followed. He was larger than Screech Owl and thought his size would protect him. He grabbed a coal in his talons and flew, but the heat singed his feathers white, and the coal fell from his grasp before he reached the earth. Hooting Owl flew home pale and ashamed.

One by one, the animals tried and failed. The larger, stronger creatures — Bear, Deer, Wolf — were too big to approach the fire without being noticed by the Thunders. The smaller creatures — Mouse, Frog, Lizard — were too weak to carry the ember. The birds, who could reach the sky world, were burned by the heat.

At last, a tiny voice spoke up from the edge of the council circle. It was Dilsdohdi — the Water Spider. She was small, no larger than a child's fist, with black downy hair marked with red stripes — the stripes, the elders say, from where the smoke and fire once touched her. She was quiet, unassuming, and no one had thought to ask her.

"I will go," said Dilsdohdi.

The animals looked at her with doubt. How could such a small creature accomplish what Bear and Raven and Owl could not? But Dilsdohdi did not argue. She spun a bowl-shaped web, strong and flexible, and placed it on her back like a basket. Then she crossed the water — for Water Spider can walk upon the surface of rivers and lakes — and climbed to the sky world.

She moved slowly, carefully, her eight legs finding footholds where no other creature could stand. When she reached the great hearth, the Thunders were elsewhere, occupied with a storm. Dilsdohdi approached the fire and placed a single, small ember in her web-basket. The heat was intense, but the web held — it was spun from the strongest silk, blessed by the spirits of the water — and Dilsdohdi carried the ember back across the water and down to the earth.

She delivered the ember to the animals, and they built the first fire on the earth. The flames leaped up, warm and bright, and the animals gathered around it, their faces golden in the light. From that fire, all other fires were lit — the cooking fires of the villages, the ceremonial fires of the medicine men, the signal fires on the mountaintops.

Dilsdohdi became the most honored of all the animals, not for her size or her strength, but for her cleverness and her courage. The Cherokee say that the Water Spider's black hair with its red stripes is the mark of her gift — the smoke and fire that touched her on the day she brought light to the world. And when you see a Water Spider skating across the surface of a lake, you are seeing the descendant of the bravest creature who ever lived.
story1055:
In the time before time, when the world was young and all living things dwelt together in harmony, the animals and the people were neighbors. They spoke the same language. They shared the same paths. The bear would nod to the hunter at the river crossing. The deer would pause at the edge of the cornfield and regard the planter with calm, knowing eyes. There was no fear between them, only a deep and ancient understanding.

But as the human population grew, something changed. The hunters became careless. They killed deer without asking forgiveness. They took more than they needed and left the rest to rot. They trapped birds for sport and crushed insects underfoot without a thought. The animals watched, and they were troubled.

The Deer held a council first. The great buck stood at the center of the gathering, his antlers crowned with autumn leaves, and he spoke with a voice that was quiet but carried the weight of mountains. "The humans have forgotten the old agreements," he said. "They take without asking. They kill without gratitude. We must remind them of the cost."

The Deer council decreed that any hunter who killed a deer without first asking the deer's spirit for forgiveness would be afflicted with rheumatism — a stiffness in the joints, a heaviness in the limbs, a pain that would remind the hunter, every day of his life, that the deer had a claim upon him.

The Birds held their council next. The Eagle, the Hawk, the Owl — they gathered in the branches of the great cedar, and they spoke of the nets and the snares and the children who stole their eggs. They decreed that humans who disturbed the nests of birds would suffer fevers, chills, and the shaking sickness.

The Insects convened in the tall grass, their council a hum of tiny voices. The Mosquito, the Fly, the Beetle — they spoke of the shoes that crushed them and the hands that swatted them. They decreed a thousand small afflictions: rashes, itches, the buzzing in the ears that drives men mad.

The Reptiles gathered by the water. The Snake, the Turtle, the Lizard — they spoke of the rocks that were overturned and the trails that were blocked. They decreed that humans who harmed reptiles would suffer from swelling, from blindness, from the creeping numbness that moves through the body like cold water.

One by one, the animal councils decreed their punishments. Disease after disease was created — each one tied to a specific offense, each one a reminder that the natural world has its own laws and its own justice.

But the Plants heard of the animals' plans. The Trees, the Herbs, the Grasses — they gathered in the forest, their leaves rustling with concern. The Plants had always been friends to the humans. They had given their branches for shelters, their bark for medicine, their fruits for food. They did not want to see the humans destroyed by the very creatures they had once lived beside.

The Plants held their own council, and they made a vow: for every disease the animals created, they would provide a cure. If the Deer decreed rheumatism, the Plants would provide a root that eased the pain. If the Birds decreed fever, the Plants would provide a leaf that brought the temperature down. If the Reptiles decreed swelling, the Plants would provide a poultice that drew it out.

And so the balance was struck. Every disease has its remedy, every affliction its cure — but only if the medicine man knows which plant to use. This is why the medicine men must spend years in the forest, learning from the spirits of the plants, memorizing the songs that open the plants' hearts and reveal their healing powers.

The Cherokee say that this is why the world is the way it is — why people get sick and why they get well, why the animals sometimes seem hostile and the plants sometimes seem to reach out a helping hand. It is all part of the great balance, the ancient agreement between the living things of the earth. To forget the agreement is to invite sickness. To remember it is to find healing.

And so the Cherokee medicine man walks through the forest with respect, greeting each plant by name, asking permission before taking a leaf or a root. He knows that every plant is a potential cure, and that every cure is a gift from the Plants who chose to be our friends.
story1056:
In the deepest caves of the Cherokee mountains, where the darkness is so complete that it seems to have weight and substance, there dwell the Stone Coats — Nûñ'yunu'ï — a race of giants whose bodies are sheathed in rock. They are ancient, older than the Cherokee, older perhaps than the mountains themselves, and they are hungry.

The Stone Coats are enormous. Their bodies tower above the trees, their shoulders broad as the side of a barn, their arms thick as the trunks of old oaks. But it is their skin that makes them invulnerable — a covering of stone, gray and rough, that fits them like armor. Arrows shatter against it. Spears crack and splinter. Even the strongest warrior's club bounces off a Stone Coat's chest with a sound like a hammer striking an anvil.

They are cannibals. The Stone Coats prey on humans who wander too deep into the remote mountains, into the caves and hollows where no hunter dares to go. They snatch travelers from the trail, crush them in their stone hands, and eat them with a terrible, grinding sound. The bones of their victims litter the floors of their caves, white and clean, picked bare.

The Stone Coats are also the kin — or at least the cousins — of Spearfinger, the witch with the stone dress. Some elders say they are the same race, that Spearfinger is simply a female Stone Coat who learned to disguise herself among humans. Others say the Stone Coats are something older and more elemental — beings of pure stone that learned to move, to hunger, to hate.

Warriors who tracked the Stone Coats reported finding their trails: great gouges in the earth where they had walked, boulders displaced and scattered like pebbles, trees snapped and bent. The Stone Coats were not careful in their movements. They did not need to be. Nothing in the forest could hurt them.

But the medicine men knew things that the warriors did not. They knew that the Stone Coats, for all their physical invulnerability, were susceptible to certain spiritual practices. A medicine man who knew the proper songs could confuse a Stone Coat, making it stumble and lose its way. A ceremony performed at the mouth of a Stone Coat's cave could封印 it, trapping it deep within the mountain.

One story tells of a village that lived in the shadow of a mountain where Stone Coats were known to dwell. Every autumn, when the leaves turned and the nights grew long, the Stone Coats would emerge from their caves and hunt. The villagers lived in fear, never venturing far from home, never walking alone in the dusk.

A young medicine man decided to end the terror. He spent a year preparing — learning the songs, gathering the herbs, fasting and praying. When autumn came, he walked to the mouth of the greatest cave and began to sing. The song was old, older than the Cherokee, older than the mountains, and it resonated with the stone itself. The cave shook. The mountain trembled. The Stone Coats inside roared and bellowed, but the song held them, drew them deeper into the earth, sealed the entrance with a force that no stone coat could break.

The village was safe — for a time. But the elders warned that the Stone Coats were not destroyed, only sleeping, and that one day they would wake.

The Cherokee say that the fossilized bones of great beasts found in the mountains — the bones of mammoths, of giant sloths, of creatures that no longer walk the earth — are the remains of the Stone Coats, or of their prey. They are reminders that the world was once ruled by giants, and that even giants can be brought low by a song and a prayer.

The Stone Coats sleep in the deep caves. But on certain nights, when the earth shakes and the rocks roll, the Cherokee say that the Nûñ'yunu'ï are stirring in their sleep, dreaming of the world above, dreaming of the taste of human flesh.
story1057:
Above the highest peaks of the Cherokee mountains, where the air is thin and the clouds gather like white rivers, there flies a bird so vast that its shadow darkens entire valleys. This is the Tlanuwa — the Giant Raptor — a creature of myth and terror, with wings that beat the sky into thunder and talons that could carry a man as easily as a hawk carries a mouse.

The Tlanuwa is not a natural bird. Its feathers are not feather but metal — iron-hard, razor-sharp, each one capable of cutting like a knife. When the Tlanuwa flies, its feathers catch the light and blaze like molten silver. When it sheds a feather, the feather falls to earth like a sword, burying itself in the ground, and the Cherokee who find these feathers know to leave them undisturbed, for they are the Tlanuwa's property, and the Tlanuwa remembers everything it has lost.

The bird's wingspan is immeasurable. Some say it stretches from one mountain peak to the next. Others say it is wider than the sky itself. When the Tlanuwa spreads its wings, the wind beneath them creates gales that tear leaves from trees and bend the grass flat against the earth. When it folds its wings and dives, it falls like a meteor, trailing fire.

The Tlanuwa lives in the highest cliffs — in caves that open onto the sky, where no human could climb and no other bird dared to nest. It feeds on deer, on bear, on anything unfortunate enough to cross its territory. The Cherokee say that in ancient times, the Tlanuwa carried off entire children, snatching them from the fields where they played and carrying them to its nest in the sky.

But the Tlanuwa's greatest enemy is the Uktena — the great horned serpent that dwells in the deep waters. The two creatures have warred since the world was young. The Tlanuwa fears the Uktena's gaze and the power of the crystal in its forehead. The Uktena fears the Tlanuwa's feathers, which can pierce even its armored scales. Their battles shake the mountains — the Tlanuwa diving from the sky, the Uktena rising from the water, their cries mixing with the thunder.

The Tlanuwa also appears in the stories of the Creek and the Natchez, which tells us something important: this creature was not unique to one tribe but was a figure of power across the entire Southeast. Each tribe understood it differently. The Cherokee saw it as a terror and a protector. The Creek saw it as a test of courage. The Natchez saw it as a messenger of the sun.

There is a story of a Cherokee village that was besieged by the Tlanuwa. The bird would circle overhead at dawn, its shadow passing over the village like a dark hand, and the people would flee to their houses and bar the doors. One brave warrior decided to face the creature. He climbed to the highest cliff where the Tlanuwa nested, carrying a bow of seasoned hickory and arrows tipped with the sharpest flint he could find.

When the Tlanuwa saw him, it screamed — a sound like metal tearing — and dove. The warrior loosed his arrow. It struck the bird's breast and glanced off the iron feathers. The Tlanuwa's talons reached for him, and he leaped aside, rolling beneath a ledge as the claws struck stone and sent sparks flying.

The warrior fought the Tlanuwa for three days and three nights. On the fourth morning, he found the creature's weakness — a single feather on the underside of its wing, a feather that had not yet hardened to iron, a feather still soft as down. He drove his arrow through the soft feather and into the wing beneath. The Tlanuwa screamed and faltered, its flight broken. It fell from the sky, and the warrior climbed down to where it lay.

The dying bird looked at the warrior with eyes that held no hatred, only a vast and ancient sadness. "You have beaten me," it said, in a voice like wind through iron reeds. "But remember: the feathers I have dropped are still mine. And I will send for them."

The warrior gathered the iron feathers and brought them to the village, where they were used to cut and scrape for generations. And the Tlanuwa's prophecy came true: every few years, a great wind would sweep through the mountains, and the feathers would vanish from the village, pulled from their hiding places by invisible hands.

The Tlanuwa still flies over the Cherokee mountains. You cannot see it — it is too high, too fast, too vast — but you can feel its shadow when the clouds gather and the wind drops and the sky goes dark in the middle of the day. That is the Tlanuwa, passing overhead, looking for what it has lost.
story1058:
The first man and the first woman had been together since the beginning, but even the first people are not immune to anger. They quarreled over something — the old stories do not say what — and the woman, her eyes blazing with a fury that could have set the forest on fire, turned her back on the man and walked away.

She walked east, toward the rising sun, and she did not look back. The man stood in the doorway of their lodge and watched her go. His heart was heavy. His pride kept him from calling after her, but his love kept him from going inside. He stood there as the sun crossed the sky, watching her figure grow smaller on the trail, until she was nothing more than a speck against the green of the forest.

The Sun saw all of this from his path across the sky. The Sun is a compassionate being — not the cold, distant disk that the later people imagine, but a warm and living presence, one who watches over the world with the care of a parent watching a child. He saw the man's sorrow and the woman's anger, and he decided to help.

As the woman walked, the Sun reached down and placed huckleberries along the path — ripe, sweet, bursting with juice. They appeared in clusters at the woman's feet, red and purple and blue, glistening in the light. But the woman was too angry to notice. She walked past the huckleberries without a glance, her eyes fixed on the horizon.

The Sun tried again. He placed blackberries along the path — fat, dark, with a sweetness that would have stopped any other traveler. The woman walked past them too, her jaw set, her feet carrying her forward with the unstoppable force of righteous anger.

The Sun paused. He had given his best gifts — the berries of the forest — and the woman had refused them. He needed something special. Something that had never existed before. Something so beautiful, so perfect, that even the angriest heart would be softened by its sight.

The Sun called upon the earth. He whispered to the soil, to the roots, to the ancient network of life that runs beneath the forest floor. And the earth answered. From the soil, from the roots, from the very bones of the world, a new plant grew. It pushed up through the leaf litter and the fallen twigs, its stem green and tender, its leaves unfurling like tiny hands.

And then the berries appeared. They were strawberries — the first strawberries that had ever existed. They were small, no larger than the tip of a child's thumb, but they were the red of a sunset, the red of a beating heart, the red of love itself. They glowed in the afternoon light like drops of blood from the earth's own veins.

The woman stopped. She looked down at the berries, and something shifted inside her — a crack in the wall of her anger, a tiny opening through which the old feelings rushed. She knelt and picked one. She held it up to the light and saw its tiny seeds, its perfect shape, its color that was the color of everything she had forgotten she loved.

She tasted it. The sweetness was like a memory — like the taste of the first meal she and the man had shared, like the sweetness of the first morning they had woken together. Tears sprang to her eyes. She gathered more berries, cradling them in her hands, and as she looked back down the path, she saw her husband approaching.

He had followed her. His pride had finally given way to his love, and he had run after her through the forest, calling her name. When they met on the path, surrounded by strawberry plants that glowed like embers in the fading light, they held each other and wept.

They returned home together, carrying the strawberries in their hands. And from that day, the strawberry has been the Cherokee symbol of reconciliation, of the sweetness that remains even after the bitterest quarrel. The elders say that the strawberry is the first berry of the season because it is the berry of first love — the love that survives anger, that endures separation, that is always, always worth coming home to.

Every spring, when the strawberries ripen in the mountains, the Cherokee hold a Strawberry Ceremony. They eat the berries and tell the story, and they remember that sweetness is stronger than anger, and that the path back to love is always lined with fruit.
